market_definition.category: Field data collection software for environmental consulting
market_definition.boundary_notes: The defining fact about this category's boundary is that it does not have a measurable one. No reliable public estimate exists for spend on field data collection software specifically; it is typically bundled into broader project management software or captured as internal IT cost [S1]. That is not a research failure to be worked around — it is a structural property of the category, and it means any sizing has to be built bottom-up from consultancy counts and observed budgets rather than found.
how_analysts_segment_it: It does not appear to be segmented as its own category at all. The available source describes the spend as absorbed into broader project management software or into internal IT cost [S1].
The buyer side is described by industry structure rather than by software category: the environmental consulting sector is highly fragmented [S1].

sizing.consensus_view: There is none, and the absence is the finding. No reliable public estimate exists for spend on field data collection software specifically [S1]. `tam_estimates` is empty because no figure was available — not because none was looked for.
sizing.cagr_range: Not established. No growth estimate for this category appears in the available material.
sizing.why_estimates_diverge: Estimates do not diverge; they do not exist. The stated reason is that the spend is bundled into broader project management software or captured as internal IT cost, so it is never measured as a separate line [S1]. A category whose spend is recorded inside someone else's budget cannot be sized from the outside.

tailwinds: Nothing in the available research establishes a tailwind. The fragmentation of the sector [S1] is consistent with uneven tooling and therefore with unmet need, but it is not evidence of demand.
headwinds: If the spend is currently internal IT cost [S1], there may be no existing software budget line to sell into, which is a materially harder sale than displacing an incumbent tool.
A highly fragmented buyer base [S1] implies many small accounts and a high cost of sale per unit of revenue.
demand_signals.buyer_budget_reality: Uncertain in a specific and consequential way: the source says this spend is typically captured as internal IT cost or bundled into project management software [S1], which suggests the budget may not exist as a separate line at all. That is the first thing a founder here should establish.

adjacent_threats: Broader project management software, which is where the source says this spend is typically bundled [S1] — the substitute is not a specialist competitor but a general tool the firm already runs.
Internally built tooling, implied by the observation that the cost is often captured as internal IT [S1].
differentiation_axes: Offline capability for remote sites, though nothing in the available research establishes whether this differentiates or is standard
Fit to environmental consulting workflow specifically, versus a general project management tool [S1]

saturation.consolidation_activity: None seen. No source addresses acquisitions in this category.
saturation.why: This read is weak and should be treated as such. No competitor of any kind is named in the available research, so `funded_competitors_known` is null rather than zero — nobody was found, which is not the same as nobody existing, and a category whose spend hides inside project management budgets [S1] is exactly the kind that would conceal its competitors from this sort of search. 'Wide-open' reflects an absence of evidence, not evidence of absence. Every one of the five saturation signals is unknown here, which is itself the most useful thing this section can report.

what_would_prevent_it: Environmental-specific workflow and regulatory reporting depth that a general project management tool would not build
Offline reliability in genuinely remote conditions, if that is technically hard rather than routine
A fragmented buyer base [S1] that gives no single platform enough share to make bundling worthwhile
absorption_risk.notes: No absorber can be named, because no platform vendor serving this sector appears anywhere in the available research. The mechanism that would matter is not acquisition by a giant but quiet substitution: the spend is already bundled into broader project management software [S1], which means a general tool may absorb the use case simply by being adequate and already installed. That is recorded as 'contested' at low confidence with no named absorber, rather than manufacturing a plausible-sounding platform. 'Unlikely this decade' refers to deliberate absorption by an identifiable acquirer; it does not describe the substitution risk just noted, which is present now.

open_source_landscape.evidence_for_the_gap: No source in this material names an open-source project in this category, reports adoption for one, or discusses open source at all. `applicable` is set false on that basis, and it should be read as unresearched rather than assessed. The capability_gap and gap_trend values are schema placeholders and carry no finding.
open_source_landscape.notes: Mobile data-collection tooling is a plausible place for open-source alternatives to exist, but nothing here establishes that they do, and inventing projects would be worse than reporting the gap.

adjacent_markets.size_note: Not sized here. The relevant fact is that field data collection spend is typically bundled into it [S1].
adjacent_markets.why_it_matters: This is where the budget already sits. A specialist tool is not entering an empty space; it is asking a firm to unbundle a line it currently pays for inside something else.
Where the cost is captured internally [S1], the alternative to buying is building or continuing manually, and there may be no purchasing process to enter at all.

economics.typical_pricing: Not established. No source gives pricing for this category.
economics.typical_gross_margin: Not established by the available research.
economics.typical_cac_payback: Not established by the available research.

funding_environment.valuation_norms: Not established. No source reports funding rounds, valuations or exits in this category.
funding_environment.notes: No funding data of any kind was available; 'steady' is the schema's least-committal option and should be read as unknown rather than as a finding.

factors: Environmental site work is typically subject to reporting requirements, which is the most likely source of workflow depth in this category — but no source in this material addresses it, so it is flagged as unexamined rather than asserted.
The structural constraint established by the evidence is budget location: the spend sits inside project management software or internal IT [S1].

sources.title: Environmental consulting industry overview
sources.what_it_supported: That the environmental consulting sector is highly fragmented, and that no reliable public estimate exists for field data collection software spend because it is bundled into broader project management software or captured as internal IT cost

research_gaps: The market cannot be sized from public sources at all [S1]. This is the central gap and it is structural: no better search would fix it. Sizing has to come from a bottom-up build — number of consultancies, seats per firm, price per seat.
No competitor of any kind was identified, so the competitive landscape is empty by absence of evidence rather than by finding. The whole competitive picture is unknown.
Whether offline-first capability differentiates in this category is not addressed anywhere.
No pricing, margin, CAC payback or contract value data exists in the material.
No funding, valuation or acquisition data.
Nothing addresses open source in this category.

Nothing speaks to the company's three pilots [C3] or to the claim that consultants collect data on paper [C2] — the latter being the premise the whole business rests on and the one most cheaply tested against the pilots.
Only one source was available for the entire analysis, which is why sizing confidence is low and why several sections report absence rather than assessment.
